Foods people use as pet names.Honey: Perhaps the most common food pet name in English; bees visit about two million flowers to make one pound of it, which suits a precious person.
Foods people use as pet names.Sugar: A sweet nickname for a loved one, and it dates back to at least the 1800s, when sugar was still a costly luxury in many places.
Foods people use as pet names.Cupcake: Cupcake as a term of endearment became popular in America in the 20th century, perhaps because the treat is small, sweet and cute.
Foods people use as pet names.Pumpkin: A classic American endearment, said to be linked to the rounded, cheerful look of the vegetable and used for small children.
Foods people use as pet names.Muffin: Calling someone muffin or stud muffin is a term of affection, probably popular because the baked good suggests warmth, softness and comfort.
Foods people use as pet names.Peach: Peach has meant a delightful person since the 1800s, and peaches are native to China, where they symbolize long life.
Foods people use as pet names.Cookie: Calling someone a cookie is affectionate in English, though a smart cookie is a clever person, and a tough cookie is hard to beat.
Foods people use as pet names.Dumpling: A plump, comforting endearment, especially in British English: apple dumpling was used affectionately for a chubby child.
Foods people use as pet names.Sweet pea: Named after a flower, not a vegetable: the sweet pea is a fragrant climbing plant, and sweetpea is used lovingly for a child or partner.
Foods people use as pet names.Honey bun: Honey bun is a sweet baked treat, and also a double-sweet nickname meaning honey plus bun, popular in the American South.
Foods people use as pet names.Cutie pie: Cutie pie dates to the 1920s or so, and combines cute with pie, which was already used as an affectionate term for something delightful.
Foods people use as pet names.Turnip: A trap: calling someone a turnip is insulting, since in British English it means a dull person; it is not a pet name.
Foods people use as pet names.Parsnip: Parsnip is a root vegetable, and sweet, but nobody uses it for a darling; in Europe it was a sweetener before sugar was common.
Foods people use as pet names.Anchovy: Tiny salty fish do not make for tender nicknames, and they were so prized in Rome they went into the fermented sauce garum.
Foods people use as pet names.Brussels sprout: These mini cabbages are a fixture of Christmas dinner, but a love interest called Brussels sprout is not a compliment; they are named for Brussels.
Foods people use as pet names.Liver: Liver is nutritious, but no one calls a sweetheart liver; the organ is among the richest sources of vitamin A and iron.
Foods people use as pet names.Sardine: Sardine is not a pet name, but it appears in the phrase packed like sardines, for crowds; the fish is named for the island of Sardinia.
Foods people use as pet names.Radish: Radish is a peppery root, not an endearment; many varieties are ready to harvest in under a month, among the fastest garden crops.
Foods people use as pet names.Kale: Kale is trendy, but no one is calling their sweetheart kale; it is a vegetable rich in vitamins K and C.
Foods people use as pet names.Tofu: Soy curd was invented in China roughly 2,000 years ago, but its blandness makes it a poor endearment for a darling.
Foods people use as pet names.Prune: Prune is a dried plum and not a darling; the California prune industry rebranded them dried plums in 2000 to improve their image.
Foods people use as pet names.Gherkin: A small pickled cucumber, and the skyscraper in London is nicknamed after it, but nobody uses it as a pet name.
Foods people use as pet names.Celery: Celery is a crunchy low-calorie snack, but it is not a name for a partner; ancient Greeks gave celery wreaths to athletes at games.
Foods people use as pet names.Lentil: Lentils are among the oldest cultivated crops, about 8,000 years, but they are not used as an endearment for a lover.

Indonesian or Malaysian dishes.Rendang: Slow-cooked in coconut milk and spices until the liquid vanishes, this Minangkabau beef dish has been ranked among the world's tastiest foods.
Indonesian or Malaysian dishes.Nasi goreng: Indonesia's fried rice gets its smoky depth from sweet soy sauce (kecap manis) and shrimp paste, often topped with a fried egg.
Indonesian or Malaysian dishes.Satay: Skewered, grilled meat served with peanut sauce; it likely grew from Javanese street vendors adapting Middle Eastern kebabs.
Indonesian or Malaysian dishes.Gado-gado: Its name means 'mix-mix': blanched vegetables, tofu and egg under a thick peanut sauce, a vegetarian-friendly Indonesian staple.
Indonesian or Malaysian dishes.Laksa: This spicy noodle soup comes in many forms, from creamy coconut curry laksa to the sour, fish-based Penang asam laksa.
Indonesian or Malaysian dishes.Nasi lemak: Rice cooked in coconut milk with anchovies, peanuts, egg and sambal; it is often called Malaysia's unofficial national dish.
Indonesian or Malaysian dishes.Mee goreng: Fried yellow noodles with chili, tomato and egg, sold by Malaysian mamak stalls and Indonesian carts alike.
Indonesian or Malaysian dishes.Roti canai: This flaky, stretchy flatbread is flipped and spun in the air like pizza dough, then dipped in dhal or curry; it descends from Indian parathas.
Indonesian or Malaysian dishes.Char kway teow: Flat rice noodles stir-fried over fierce heat in a wok, giving the 'wok hei' smokiness Penang's hawkers are famous for.
Indonesian or Malaysian dishes.Tempeh: Whole soybeans bound into a firm cake by a mold, Rhizopus; this fermented Javanese food is a protein-rich meat alternative.
Indonesian or Malaysian dishes.Sambal: Indonesia and Malaysia have hundreds of versions of this chili paste, and many households prize their own recipe.
Indonesian or Malaysian dishes.Soto ayam: A turmeric-yellow Indonesian chicken soup with glass noodles and egg, often finished with a squeeze of lime and a spoonful of sambal.
Indonesian or Malaysian dishes.Adobo: Though it may seem close, this is the Philippines' vinegar-and-soy braise, often called the unofficial national dish, so it's not from Indonesia or Malaysia.
Indonesian or Malaysian dishes.Pho: A trap for noodle soup fans: this beef or chicken noodle soup is Vietnamese, from Hanoi, not Indonesian or Malaysian.
Indonesian or Malaysian dishes.Pad thai: Thailand's stir-fried rice noodles were promoted in the 1930s-40s to build national identity, so this is Thai rather than Indonesian.
Indonesian or Malaysian dishes.Banh mi: This sandwich is Vietnamese, with a French-style baguette from colonial history stuffed with pickled vegetables, herbs and pork.
Indonesian or Malaysian dishes.Tom yum: This hot-and-sour soup is Thai, built on lemongrass, galangal and kaffir lime leaves, so it doesn't belong on the Indonesian-Malaysian list.
Indonesian or Malaysian dishes.Bibimbap: Korean for 'mixed rice', this bowl of rice, vegetables and egg is stirred together with gochujang; it is Korean, not Southeast Asian maritime.
Indonesian or Malaysian dishes.Ramen: Japan's wheat noodle soup has Chinese roots and became hugely popular after World War II; it is not an Indonesian or Malaysian dish.
Indonesian or Malaysian dishes.Pancit: The Philippines' noodle dishes, brought by Chinese traders, are served at birthdays to symbolize long life, but they aren't Indonesian or Malaysian.
Indonesian or Malaysian dishes.Bulgogi: Marinated, thinly sliced beef grilled at the table, bulgogi is Korean; the name literally means 'fire meat'.
Indonesian or Malaysian dishes.Sinigang: A sour Filipino stew, commonly soured with tamarind, which is why it might trick you, yet it is from the Philippines.
Indonesian or Malaysian dishes.Som tam: Pounded in a mortar, this green papaya salad comes from Thailand and Laos, not Indonesia or Malaysia.
Indonesian or Malaysian dishes.Massaman curry: A Thai curry showing Persian and Muslim influence with potatoes and peanuts; it is Thai, though near neighbors share the spices.

Indian sweets.Gulab jamun: Fried milk-solid dumplings soaked in rose-scented syrup, the name pairs Persian for rose water with the jamun fruit they resemble.
Indian sweets.Jalebi: Spirals of batter are deep-fried and dunked in saffron syrup; the dessert is thought to trace to Persian zalabiya.
Indian sweets.Rasgulla: Spongy cheese balls in light syrup, whose origin Odisha and West Bengal have both claimed, and both hold official protected status for it.
Indian sweets.Barfi: A dense fudge-like sweet made from condensed milk, often decorated with edible silver leaf called varak.
Indian sweets.Ladoo: These round sweets, made from flour, ghee and sugar, are offered at temples and festivals, with motichoor ladoo being a favorite.
Indian sweets.Kheer: Rice slow-cooked in milk with sugar, cardamom and nuts; this pudding is offered to deities and served at celebrations.
Indian sweets.Kulfi: Dense, slow-frozen Indian ice cream, made without churning, from reduced milk, often flavored with pistachio or cardamom.
Indian sweets.Rasmalai: Soft cheese patties floating in saffron-cardamom thickened milk, a Bengali creation served chilled.
Indian sweets.Peda: Soft, fudgy milk sweets from Mathura, often pressed into discs and flavored with cardamom or saffron.
Indian sweets.Mysore pak: A rich fudge of gram flour, ghee and sugar was first made in the royal kitchens of the Mysore palace.
Indian sweets.Soan papdi: Flaky, thread-like layers of gram flour and sugar make a sweet that crumbles into airy strands, often given at Diwali.
Indian sweets.Gajar ka halwa: Grated carrots simmered in milk, sugar and ghee make this winter pudding, a staple at Indian weddings and festivals.
Indian sweets.Baklava: Layers of filo with nuts and syrup are a Middle Eastern and Balkan pastry, with Turkey and Greece both claiming it, not Indian.
Indian sweets.Mochi: Pounded glutinous rice cake from Japan, not India, and a New Year tradition there.
Indian sweets.Churros: Fried dough sticks from Spain and Latin America, usually dipped in hot chocolate, not Indian.
Indian sweets.Tiramisu: Italy's coffee-soaked dessert, whose name means 'pick me up'.
Indian sweets.Flan: Caramel custard of Spanish and Latin American fame, not Indian.
Indian sweets.Turkish delight: Chewy, starch-and-sugar lokum from Ottoman Turkey, famously the White Witch's bait in Narnia.
Indian sweets.Brownie: An American chocolate square invented in the late 1800s, and not an Indian sweet.
Indian sweets.Macaron: This French meringue sandwich cookie is made with almond flour; it isn't Indian.
Indian sweets.Kunafa: A cheese pastry of shredded dough soaked in syrup, popular in the Middle East, not India.
Indian sweets.Mooncake: Dense, filled Chinese pastry eaten at the Mid-Autumn Festival.
Indian sweets.Cannoli: Fried pastry tubes filled with sweet ricotta from Sicily, Italian rather than Indian.
Indian sweets.Alfajores: South American dulce de leche sandwich cookies, even though the name has Arabic roots, are not Indian.

Animals native to South America.Sloth: Sloths are so slow that algae grows on their fur, giving them a greenish tinge that helps camouflage them.
Animals native to South America.Llama: Llamas were domesticated in the Andes thousands of years ago, and they hum to communicate with each other.
Animals native to South America.Alpaca: Alpacas are bred for their soft fleece in the Andes, and they differ from llamas by being smaller with shorter faces.
Animals native to South America.Jaguar: Jaguars are the largest cats in the Americas, and they love water, often hunting caimans in rivers.
Animals native to South America.Toucan: Toucans have huge, light beaks that help them regulate their body heat, and live in tropical forests from Mexico to Argentina.
Animals native to South America.Capybara: The capybara is the world's largest rodent, can weigh about 60 kg, and often sleeps while sitting in water.
Animals native to South America.Anaconda: The green anaconda is the heaviest snake, found in Amazon swamps and rivers, and females are much larger than males.
Animals native to South America.Piranha: Piranhas live in South American rivers, and attacks on people are rare; they mostly scavenge.
Animals native to South America.Andean condor: The Andean condor is one of the world's largest flying birds, and it can ride air currents for hours.
Animals native to South America.Armadillo: Armadillo means 'little armoured one' in Spanish, and the three-banded kind can roll itself into a ball.
Animals native to South America.Poison dart frog: Poison dart frogs of Central and South American rainforests are tiny and bright, and Indigenous people used their toxins on blowgun darts.
Animals native to South America.Giant anteater: A giant anteater can eat up to about 30,000 ants and termites in a day, with a tongue that flicks about 150 times a minute.
Animals native to South America.Lion: Lions live in Africa, plus a small population in India, and not in the Americas.
Animals native to South America.Tiger: Tigers are Asian big cats, not South American, and the Amazon has jaguars instead.
Animals native to South America.Kangaroo: Kangaroos are native to Australia and New Guinea, not South America.
Animals native to South America.Gorilla: Gorillas live in the forests of central Africa, not the Americas.
Animals native to South America.Koala: Koalas live in eastern Australia, and their fingerprints are remarkably similar to humans'.
Animals native to South America.Panda: Pandas are native to the mountains of central China, not South America.
Animals native to South America.Hippo: Hippos live in Africa's rivers and lakes, and not in the Americas, apart from Pablo Escobar's escaped herd in Colombia.
Animals native to South America.Camel: Camels are native to Africa and Asia; the South American relatives are llamas and alpacas, but they aren't camels.
Animals native to South America.Lemur: Lemurs live only on Madagascar, not in South America.
Animals native to South America.Zebra: Zebras roam Africa's grasslands, and none lives wild in South America.
Animals native to South America.Orangutan: Orangutans are found only in Borneo and Sumatra, not in South America.
Animals native to South America.Okapi: The okapi lives only in the forests of the Democratic Republic of Congo.

Animals in the Chinese zodiac.Rat: Rats are in the Chinese zodiac, in first place. A legend says the rat rode on the Ox's back and jumped ahead at the finish of the Jade Emperor's race.
Animals in the Chinese zodiac.Ox: The Ox is the second sign, linked to diligence and honesty. It's said the ox arrived second, but carried the rat across.
Animals in the Chinese zodiac.Tiger: The Tiger is third in the zodiac and stands for bravery. In China, the markings on its forehead are said to resemble the character for 'king'.
Animals in the Chinese zodiac.Rabbit: The Rabbit is fourth, a symbol of luck and gentleness. In Vietnam, the Cat takes its place in the zodiac.
Animals in the Chinese zodiac.Dragon: The Dragon is the only mythical creature among the twelve. It's seen as the most auspicious sign, and birth rates often jump in Dragon years.
Animals in the Chinese zodiac.Snake: The Snake is the sixth sign, thought of as wise and mysterious. It is said to have beaten the Horse by hiding in its hoof.
Animals in the Chinese zodiac.Horse: The Horse is the seventh sign, linked with energy and freedom. In the legend it was nearly first, but was surprised by the Snake.
Animals in the Chinese zodiac.Goat: The Goat, also called Sheep or Ram, is the eighth sign. English-language lists vary because Chinese 'yang' covers all of them.
Animals in the Chinese zodiac.Monkey: The Monkey is the ninth sign, and stands for cleverness. In the legend, it helped others across the river.
Animals in the Chinese zodiac.Rooster: The Rooster is the tenth sign, tied to punctuality and pride. It is the only bird in the zodiac.
Animals in the Chinese zodiac.Dog: The Dog is the eleventh sign, a symbol of loyalty. In the tale, it was late despite being a great swimmer, because it stopped for a bath.
Animals in the Chinese zodiac.Pig: The Pig is the twelfth and last sign. In the legend, it overslept after eating a big meal, and nearly missed the race.
Animals in the Chinese zodiac.Cat: The cat is the famous absentee. One story says the rat tricked it, so it missed the race, which is why cats chase rats.
Animals in the Chinese zodiac.Lion: The lion is not in the zodiac. The Chinese zodiac is made of animals familiar to ancient Chinese farming life, and lions were not.
Animals in the Chinese zodiac.Elephant: The elephant is absent from the zodiac, though it figures in other Asian traditions. In Thailand, white elephants are considered sacred.
Animals in the Chinese zodiac.Bear: The bear isn't part of the zodiac. It features instead in other cultural traditions, like the Ainu people's reverence of bears.
Animals in the Chinese zodiac.Duck: The duck is not in the zodiac, though the Mandarin duck is a Chinese symbol of marital fidelity.
Animals in the Chinese zodiac.Panda: The panda is China's national treasure, but not a zodiac sign. The zodiac was set well before the panda became a symbol.
Animals in the Chinese zodiac.Wolf: The wolf is absent from the Chinese zodiac. In the Turkic and Mongol traditions, though, it's a revered ancestor.
Animals in the Chinese zodiac.Fox: The fox does not appear in the Chinese zodiac. In East Asian folklore, foxes shapeshift and gain tails with age, up to nine.
Animals in the Chinese zodiac.Deer: The deer is not in the zodiac, but is a symbol of longevity in Chinese culture. The word for deer sounds like that for prosperity.
Animals in the Chinese zodiac.Crane: The crane is not a zodiac animal, but is a Chinese symbol of long life. Japanese tradition says folding 1,000 paper cranes grants a wish.
Animals in the Chinese zodiac.Turtle: The turtle is absent from the zodiac, but is a figure in Chinese mythology. It's one of the Four Benevolent Animals, and stands for longevity.
Animals in the Chinese zodiac.Fish: Fish aren't among the twelve zodiac animals, though they're a symbol of abundance. The word for fish sounds like the word for surplus.

French dishes.Ratatouille: A Provençal vegetable stew that became a film star when a rat chef in a Pixar movie served a refined version.
French dishes.Bouillabaisse: A Marseille fish stew, traditionally made with the rockfish too bony to sell, and served with rouille and bread.
French dishes.Coq au vin: Chicken braised in red wine with bacon, mushrooms and onions, a dish that was popularised in America by Julia Child.
French dishes.Cassoulet: A slow-baked casserole of white beans, sausage and duck confit from southwest France; each town argues about the true recipe.
French dishes.Boeuf bourguignon: Beef stewed in red Burgundy wine with mushrooms and onions, which Julia Child made famous in America.
French dishes.Quiche Lorraine: A savoury custard tart from Lorraine; the original has bacon and eggs and cream, but, tradition says, no cheese.
French dishes.Croque monsieur: A grilled ham and cheese sandwich first served in Paris cafés in 1910; with a fried egg on top it becomes a 'croque madame'.
French dishes.Confit de canard: Duck legs slowly cooked and preserved in their own fat, a technique that kept meat through winters before refrigeration.
French dishes.Soufflé: The name means 'puffed'; whisked egg whites trap air that expands in the oven, so the dish rises, then deflates minutes after.
French dishes.Tarte Tatin: An upside-down caramelised apple tart said to have been created by accident by the Tatin sisters at their hotel.
French dishes.Escargots: Snails cooked in garlic and parsley butter; France eats tens of thousands of tonnes of snails each year.
French dishes.Gratin dauphinois: Sliced potatoes baked slowly in cream and garlic; in the authentic version from Dauphiné there is no cheese.
French dishes.Crêpes: Thin pancakes from Brittany, eaten on Candlemas, when tradition says you should flip the pancake while holding a coin.
French dishes.Risotto: Italian rice cooked in broth, so it's not French.
French dishes.Paella: A Spanish rice dish from Valencia, traditionally cooked in a wide shallow pan, so it is not French.
French dishes.Goulash: A Hungarian stew seasoned with paprika, which began as a herdsmen's meal, so it is not French.
French dishes.Schnitzel: A breaded cutlet from Austria and Germany, not French.
French dishes.Moussaka: A Greek aubergine and meat bake, not French.
French dishes.Poutine: A Canadian dish from Quebec, a French-speaking province, but not French cuisine.
French dishes.Eggs Benedict: An American brunch dish, though its sauce, hollandaise, is French in style, and the dish was created in New York.
French dishes.Pierogi: Polish filled dumplings, boiled and often pan-fried afterwards, so they are not French.
French dishes.Tagine: A North African stew, not French, though it is commonly eaten in France.
French dishes.Gazpacho: A cold Spanish tomato soup from Andalusia, so not French, though France has chilled soups such as vichyssoise.
French dishes.Carbonara: An Italian pasta with eggs, cheese and cured pork, not French.

Foods named after places.Hamburger: The hamburger is named for Hamburg, Germany, yet the ground-beef sandwich in a bun took its modern form in the United States.
Foods named after places.Frankfurter: Frankfurters trace to Frankfurt, Germany, and the hot dog's other name, wiener, comes from Vienna, whose German name is Wien.
Foods named after places.Champagne: Only sparkling wine from France's Champagne region may legally carry the name in the EU, and it's protected by strict law.
Foods named after places.Cheddar: Cheddar comes from the English village of Cheddar in Somerset, where cheese was once aged in the nearby limestone caves of Cheddar Gorge.
Foods named after places.Parmesan: Parmesan means 'from Parma', and the real Parmigiano-Reggiano is aged at least 12 months under strict rules.
Foods named after places.Bologna: Bologna sausage is named for the Italian city of Bologna, whose own mortadella is the ancestor of the American lunch meat.
Foods named after places.Dijon mustard: Dijon mustard comes from Dijon in Burgundy, France, and the style traditionally uses verjuice or white wine instead of vinegar.
Foods named after places.Buffalo wings: Buffalo wings are named for Buffalo, New York, where they were first served in the 1960s at the Anchor Bar, and the buffalo isn't an ingredient.
Foods named after places.Gouda: Gouda is named after a Dutch town, though the cheese was traditionally sold at the market there rather than made in the town itself.
Foods named after places.Tangerine: The tangerine is named for Tangier, Morocco, the port from which the fruit was shipped to Europe and America.
Foods named after places.Camembert: Camembert is named after a village in Normandy, and legend credits a farmer, Marie Harel, with its creation.
Foods named after places.Brussels sprouts: Brussels sprouts are named after Brussels, Belgium, where they were grown widely from the 1500s and have been cultivated for centuries.
Foods named after places.Baked Alaska: Baked Alaska, a cake with ice cream under a meringue shell, was named for the US purchase of Alaska in 1867.
Foods named after places.Caesar salad: Caesar salad was named for Caesar Cardini, an Italian-born restaurateur in Tijuana, Mexico, not for Julius Caesar or the Roman Empire.
Foods named after places.Eggs Benedict: Eggs Benedict is named for a person, though who is disputed: a New York socialite, Lemuel Benedict, claimed to have invented it in the 1890s.
Foods named after places.Nachos: Nachos are named after Ignacio 'Nacho' Anaya, a restaurant maitre d' in Piedras Negras, Mexico, who improvised them around 1943.
Foods named after places.Margherita pizza: Margherita pizza honors Queen Margherita of Savoy, who was served the red, white and green pizza in Naples in 1889.
Foods named after places.Pavlova: Pavlova honors the ballerina Anna Pavlova, and both Australia and New Zealand claim to have invented the meringue dessert.
Foods named after places.Peach Melba: Peach Melba was created by Escoffier for the Australian soprano Nellie Melba, so it's named for her and not for a place.
Foods named after places.Earl Grey: Earl Grey tea probably honors Charles Grey, the 2nd Earl Grey and British prime minister, and it's flavored with bergamot oil.
Foods named after places.Bellini: The Bellini cocktail is named for the Venetian painter Giovanni Bellini, since its pink tint reminded its inventor of one of his paintings.
Foods named after places.Carpaccio: Carpaccio is named for the Venetian painter Vittore Carpaccio, whose reds recalled the raw beef slices, and it first appeared at Harry's Bar.
Foods named after places.Fettuccine Alfredo: Fettuccine Alfredo is named for Alfredo di Lelio, a Roman restaurateur, who made it for his wife in the 1900s.
Foods named after places.Cobb salad: Cobb salad was named for Robert Cobb, owner of the Hollywood Brown Derby restaurant, where it was supposedly thrown together late at night.

Recipes that need eggs.Mayonnaise: Egg yolk is the emulsifier holding oil and vinegar together. Without it, the sauce splits into greasy puddles.
Recipes that need eggs.Meringue: Whipped egg whites and sugar. Any trace of yolk fat will stop the whites from rising into stiff peaks.
Recipes that need eggs.Hollandaise: Warm egg yolks whisked with melted butter and lemon. Overheat it and the yolks scramble.
Recipes that need eggs.Custard: Egg yolks thicken milk as they gently cook at around 80 C. Above that, the mixture curdles.
Recipes that need eggs.Carbonara: Roman pasta where egg yolks, cheese and pasta water form a creamy sauce. Cream is not traditional.
Recipes that need eggs.Quiche: A savory egg custard baked in pastry. The name is from Lorraine in France, and the Germans called it kuchen.
Recipes that need eggs.Eggnog: A festive drink of milk, cream, sugar and eggs, often spiked with rum or brandy. It likely descended from medieval British posset.
Recipes that need eggs.Soufflé: The French word means puffed up. Beaten egg whites trap air that expands when heated and then collapses within minutes.
Recipes that need eggs.Pavlova: Meringue with a crisp shell and marshmallow center, topped with fruit. Australia and New Zealand dispute who invented it.
Recipes that need eggs.French toast: Bread soaked in egg and milk and fried. It is old: a Roman cookbook has a similar recipe, and it is not originally French.
Recipes that need eggs.Zabaglione: Italian dessert of egg yolks, sugar and sweet wine whisked over heat. In France, it is called sabayon.
Recipes that need eggs.Crème brûlée: Egg yolk custard with a hard caramelized sugar crust. The French name means burnt cream.
Recipes that need eggs.Eggs Benedict: Poached eggs and ham on English muffins under hollandaise. Both New York restaurants claim its origins.
Recipes that need eggs.Omelette: Beaten eggs cooked in a pan. French chefs famously judge cooks by their omelette skill.
Recipes that need eggs.Hummus: Chickpeas, tahini, lemon and garlic with no eggs. It's naturally vegan.
Recipes that need eggs.Guacamole: Mashed avocado, lime and salt. The name comes from Nahuatl, meaning avocado sauce.
Recipes that need eggs.Vinaigrette: Oil and vinegar whisked together. Mustard is often added to help it emulsify, with no eggs required.
Recipes that need eggs.Tahini: Ground sesame seeds, nothing else needed. It is naturally an emulsion of oil and solids.
Recipes that need eggs.Jam: Fruit, sugar and pectin boiled until it sets. No egg is needed.
Recipes that need eggs.Ketchup: Tomatoes, vinegar and sugar. Early English ketchups were made from mushrooms or fish brine instead.
Recipes that need eggs.Popcorn: Corn kernels heated in a pot, with no egg. The heated moisture explodes the hull.
Recipes that need eggs.Tzatziki: Greek yogurt, cucumber, garlic and olive oil. Dairy but no eggs.
Recipes that need eggs.Gazpacho: Chilled Spanish soup of raw tomato, peppers and bread. It contains no eggs.
Recipes that need eggs.Egg cream: A New York soda fountain drink made with milk, seltzer and chocolate syrup. It contains neither egg nor cream.

Rivers of Asia.Ganges: Hindus consider the river holy, and millions bathe in it at the Kumbh Mela. It's about 2,500 km long and home to rare freshwater dolphins.
Rivers of Asia.Yangtze: Asia's longest river runs about 6,300 km across China. The Three Gorges Dam on it is the largest hydroelectric project ever built.
Rivers of Asia.Mekong: It winds through six countries and supports one of the world's biggest inland fisheries. In its delta, floating markets sell produce from boats.
Rivers of Asia.Indus: It gave its name to India and to the Indus Valley civilization, which built planned cities 4,500 years ago. It flows mostly through Pakistan.
Rivers of Asia.Yellow River: Called the cradle of Chinese civilization, it carries so much silt that it turns yellow. Its floods have shifted course and killed millions.
Rivers of Asia.Brahmaputra: It runs from Tibet through India to Bangladesh. At times it is so wide in Assam that it holds one of the world's largest river islands, Majuli.
Rivers of Asia.Irrawaddy: Myanmar's lifeline flows over 2,000 km to the Andaman Sea. Freshwater dolphins of the same name swim in its waters.
Rivers of Asia.Ob: A Siberian giant, flowing north to the Arctic. Together with its tributary the Irtysh, it forms one of the longest river systems in the world.
Rivers of Asia.Lena: One of the biggest Siberian rivers, it empties into the Arctic Ocean through a vast delta. Its pillars of rock stand as a World Heritage site.
Rivers of Asia.Amur: It forms much of the border between Russia and China, and is home to a rare Siberian tiger habitat and giant sturgeon called kaluga.
Rivers of Asia.Tigris: With the Euphrates, it defined Mesopotamia, the land between the rivers. Baghdad sits on its banks, and its name means swift.
Rivers of Asia.Euphrates: This is the longest river in Western Asia. Its water fed the first cities of Sumer, and it's mentioned in the Bible and in Babylonian records.
Rivers of Asia.Yenisei: One of Siberia's great rivers, and it's the largest river flowing into the Arctic Ocean. It runs from Mongolia across Russia.
Rivers of Asia.Danube: A European river that flows through ten countries, and not Asia. Its mouth is in Romania and Ukraine on the Black Sea.
Rivers of Asia.Volga: Europe's longest river, in Russia, flowing south to the Caspian Sea. It is considered to lie in Europe, not Asia.
Rivers of Asia.Nile: It flows north through northeast Africa. The Blue and White Niles meet at Khartoum.
Rivers of Asia.Amazon: The world's largest river by volume flows through South America.
Rivers of Asia.Rhine: The major river of western Europe runs from the Swiss Alps to the North Sea, famed for its castles and wine slopes.
Rivers of Asia.Zambezi: This southern African river is home to Victoria Falls, and runs through Zambia and Zimbabwe.
Rivers of Asia.Congo: The river is Africa's deepest, which flows through Central Africa and across the equator twice.

Changes of state (phase changes).Melting: Solid turning to liquid; ice stays at 0 degrees C while melting, because all the added heat goes into breaking bonds.
Changes of state (phase changes).Freezing: Liquid becomes solid; water is unusual because it expands as it freezes, which is why ice floats and pipes burst.
Changes of state (phase changes).Boiling: Liquid to gas throughout the liquid; water boils at a lower temperature on mountains, so eggs take longer to cook there.
Changes of state (phase changes).Evaporation: Liquid to gas from the surface, at any temperature; it's how sweat cools you and puddles vanish.
Changes of state (phase changes).Condensation: Gas becoming liquid, as on a cold glass; the same process builds clouds, and dew is one result.
Changes of state (phase changes).Sublimation: Solid turning straight into gas; dry ice does it, and so does snow slowly vanishing in cold dry air.
Changes of state (phase changes).Deposition: Gas going straight to solid, with no liquid step; frost on a window forms this way.
Changes of state (phase changes).Vaporization: The umbrella word for liquid turning into gas, covering both boiling and evaporation.
Changes of state (phase changes).Solidification: Another name for freezing; molten metal does it when casting, and it often releases heat as it sets.
Changes of state (phase changes).Thawing: Frozen things warming back to liquid; frozen food thaws, as does Arctic permafrost, which stores huge amounts of carbon.
Changes of state (phase changes).Erosion: A trap: wearing away of land by water, wind or ice. Rock changes place, not state; the Grand Canyon is the grand result.
Changes of state (phase changes).Oxidation: A trap: a chemical reaction with oxygen, like rust. The substance becomes a new one, not just a new state.
Changes of state (phase changes).Combustion: A trap: burning creates new substances such as CO2 and water, so it's a chemical change, not a phase change.
Changes of state (phase changes).Fermentation: A trap: microbes turn sugars to alcohol or acid, a chemical change that makes bread rise and wine.
Changes of state (phase changes).Photosynthesis: A trap: plants turn CO2 and water into sugar and oxygen using light, which is a chemical reaction, not a phase change.
Changes of state (phase changes).Rusting: A trap: iron reacts with oxygen and water to form flaky iron oxide, a new compound and not a phase change.
Changes of state (phase changes).Dissolving: A trap: sugar in tea spreads out but is still sugar, and it is not a change of state; it's mixing.
Changes of state (phase changes).Diffusion: A trap: particles spreading from crowded to empty areas, like perfume across a room. No state changes.
Changes of state (phase changes).Osmosis: A trap: water moving through a membrane toward saltier side; it's how plant roots draw in water, not a phase change.
Changes of state (phase changes).Corrosion: A trap: metals slowly breaking down chemically, like green copper on the Statue of Liberty.
Changes of state (phase changes).Digestion: A trap: your body breaks food into new molecules with enzymes, which is chemical, not a state change.
Changes of state (phase changes).Respiration: A trap: cells burn glucose with oxygen to release energy, a chemical process rather than a phase change.
Changes of state (phase changes).Decomposition: A trap: fungi and bacteria break dead matter into simpler substances, making new chemicals rather than changing states.
Changes of state (phase changes).Neutralization: A trap: an acid and a base react to make salt and water, which is a chemical change, not a phase one.

Characters in Monsters Inc..Mike Wazowski: The one-eyed green scarer is basically a round head on two legs. Billy Crystal improvised so much that animators built scenes around his takes.
Characters in Monsters Inc..Boo: The toddler whose touch terrifies monsters. Mary Gibbs, who voiced her, was about two and a half, and the recordings came from her playing in the studio.
Characters in Monsters Inc..Randall: The lizard-like rival who can turn invisible. He is the film's villain, whose chameleon-style camouflage was a showcase for Pixar's rendering.
Characters in Monsters Inc..Celia: Mike's girlfriend, whose hair is a nest of snakes. She works at the Monsters, Inc. front desk, where the snakes complain about being ignored.
Characters in Monsters Inc..Roz: The slug-like clerk at the filing desk who is secretly the agent of the Child Detection Agency. Her hoarse voice belongs to Bob Peterson, a Pixar story artist.
Characters in Monsters Inc..Mr. Waternoose: The company's boss, who is a many-legged monster who wants to kidnap children to fix the energy shortage. He is the real villain.
Characters in Monsters Inc..Fungus: Randall's assistant, voiced by Frank Oz, the Muppet performer who also gave voice to Yoda and Miss Piggy.
Characters in Monsters Inc..Yeti: The abominable snowman who lives in the Himalayas and sells snow cones. John Ratzenberger voices him, as he does in nearly every Pixar film.
Characters in Monsters Inc..George Sanderson: The monster with a sock stuck to his back, which sets off the film's decontamination alarm. It's a gag that fuels the climax.
Characters in Monsters Inc..Oscar the Grouch: This is Sesame Street, not Monsters, Inc. Oscar lives in a trash can and was originally orange before turning green in 1970.
Characters in Monsters Inc..Cookie Monster: Sesame Street's blue muppet is not from Monsters, Inc. He is a different monster who loves cookies, and who gets very emotional about them.
Characters in Monsters Inc..Grover: Sesame Street's blue monster Grover is not a Monsters, Inc. character. He is a super hero in disguise, called Super Grover.

Characters in Monsters Inc..Stitch: Stitch is an alien from Lilo and Stitch, not a Monsters, Inc. character. He was designed as an unstoppable experiment.
Characters in Monsters Inc..Frankenstein: Frankenstein's monster is a classic horror monster, not a Monsters, Inc. character. The real Frankenstein was the doctor.

Characters in Monsters Inc..Ludo: Ludo is the horned monster in Labyrinth, the 1986 Jim Henson film. A big, gentle monster like Sulley, but from a different film.

Characters in Alice in Wonderland.Alice: Lewis Carroll based her on Alice Liddell, a real girl he told the story to on a rowing trip in 1862.
Characters in Alice in Wonderland.Mad Hatter: Carroll never calls him that in the book, only 'the Hatter'. Hatters did suffer mercury poisoning, which caused tremors, giving 'mad as a hatter'.
Characters in Alice in Wonderland.March Hare: His madness refers to the hare's wild behavior during mating season in March, which inspired the English saying 'mad as a March hare'.
Characters in Alice in Wonderland.Cheshire Cat: The cat's grin was already a proverb, 'to grin like a Cheshire cat', when Carroll gave it a face that vanishes last.
Characters in Alice in Wonderland.White Rabbit: The waistcoated, watch-checking rabbit is what first draws Alice down the hole. In the book he is perpetually late.
Characters in Alice in Wonderland.Queen of Hearts: Her cry of 'Off with their heads!' is the best-known line, though in the book the King quietly pardons most of the condemned.
Characters in Alice in Wonderland.Caterpillar: He sits on a mushroom smoking a hookah and asks Alice the famous question, 'Who are you?'
Characters in Alice in Wonderland.Dormouse: Constantly asleep at the tea party, he is eventually stuffed into a teapot to be quiet.
Characters in Alice in Wonderland.Tweedledum: He and Tweedledee come from Through the Looking-Glass, not the first book, and they come from an old nursery rhyme.
Characters in Alice in Wonderland.Tweedledee: A twin who loves to quarrel with Tweedledum over a rattle, the pair were taken from a nursery rhyme about a spoiled rattle.
Characters in Alice in Wonderland.Dodo: The extinct bird is thought to be a nod to Carroll, whose real name, Charles Dodgson, he stuttered, 'Do-Do-Dodgson'.
Characters in Alice in Wonderland.King of Hearts: The mild monarch lets the Queen's death sentences slide by quietly pardoning prisoners behind her back.
Characters in Alice in Wonderland.Bill the Lizard: A hapless lizard who gets sent up the chimney, then kicked out by Alice, appearing in the White Rabbit's house.
Characters in Alice in Wonderland.Dorothy: She's from The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, by L. Frank Baum, not Carroll's Wonderland. Both involve a girl in a strange land.
Characters in Alice in Wonderland.Toto: Dorothy's dog belongs to Oz. In the 1939 film he was played by a Cairn terrier named Terry, who earned more than many actors.
Characters in Alice in Wonderland.Scarecrow: Oz, not Wonderland: he wants a brain, but proves plenty clever with the other characters in the books and film.
Characters in Alice in Wonderland.Tin Man: The Oz character in Baum's book is the Tin Woodman, a man gradually replaced by tin parts after a witch's curse.
Characters in Alice in Wonderland.Glinda: The good witch of Oz is a Baum creation. In the 1939 film, she arrives in a floating bubble.
Characters in Alice in Wonderland.Aslan: The lion belongs to The Chronicles of Narnia by C. S. Lewis, who was a friend and fellow Oxford writer of J. R. R. Tolkien.
Characters in Alice in Wonderland.Mr. Tumnus: A faun from Narnia, who greets Lucy at a lamppost. Lewis said the book began with just this image of a faun in a snowy wood.
Characters in Alice in Wonderland.White Witch: Narnia's villain Jadis is a C. S. Lewis creation, so she has no place in Carroll's Wonderland, though the Queen of Hearts is similarly tyrannical.
Characters in Alice in Wonderland.Tinker Bell: The fairy belongs to J. M. Barrie's Peter Pan, where she is nearly killed by poison. In the play audiences clapped to save her.
Characters in Alice in Wonderland.Captain Hook: Pan's pirate captain was a Barrie creation. He's afraid of the crocodile that ate his hand.
Characters in Alice in Wonderland.Jiminy Cricket: Disney's 1940 Pinocchio invented the conscience, as the original book's cricket gets squashed early on.

Yoga poses.Lotus: The classic seated meditation posture, which needs very flexible hips, and forcing it can injure the knees.
Yoga poses.Mountain: Tadasana looks like simply standing, but it is the base for many other poses, and focuses on alignment.
Yoga poses.Cat-cow: A flowing pair of poses, alternately arching and rounding the spine, usually used as a warm-up.
Yoga poses.Bridge: Lifting the hips from lying down, a pose that works the glutes and opens the chest, called Setu Bandhasana.
Yoga poses.Corpse: Savasana, lying flat on the back, is the final relaxation, and many teachers consider it the hardest to do well, because it requires stillness.
Yoga poses.Pigeon: A deep hip opener where one leg bends in front while the other stretches behind, a pose that often draws surprising emotional release.
Yoga poses.Crow: An arm balance with the knees resting on the upper arms, where beginners often topple forward.
Yoga poses.Triangle: Trikonasana is a standing side stretch, with the legs wide and one arm reaching up and the other down.
Yoga poses.Burpee: A trap: this squat-thrust-jump was invented in the 1930s by physiologist Royal Burpee as a fitness test, not a yoga pose.
Yoga poses.Jumping jack: A calisthenic exercise, where it is also known as a star jump, but not a yoga pose.
Yoga poses.Sit-up: A core exercise from fitness classes, not from yoga.
Yoga poses.Deadlift: A barbell lift from strength training, which is not part of yoga.
Yoga poses.Bicep curl: A dumbbell move for the arms, found in gyms, not yoga studios.
Yoga poses.Pull-up: A bodyweight strength move, performed on a bar, and not a yoga pose.
Yoga poses.Bench press: A barbell lift where you lie on a bench, which is a gym staple and not yoga.
Yoga poses.Crunch: An abdominal exercise from gym classes, with no yoga equivalent.
Yoga poses.Mountain climber: Despite sharing 'mountain' in name, it's a fast cardio move, not Tadasana, the yoga Mountain pose.
Yoga poses.Kettlebell swing: A gym lift using a cast-iron weight with a handle, which is traditional in Russian strength training, and it isn't yoga.
Yoga poses.Box jump: A plyometric exercise for jumping onto a platform, not a yoga pose.

Minecraft blocks and items.Diamond: Diamonds are the rare ore that gives you the strongest tools short of Netherite. Mining them at a low depth is the classic goal for new players.
Minecraft blocks and items.Redstone: Redstone is Minecraft's wiring, with dust carrying signals that players use to build working calculators and even computers.
Minecraft blocks and items.Obsidian: You make obsidian by water meeting lava, and need a diamond pickaxe to mine it. A frame of it is used to build a Nether portal.
Minecraft blocks and items.Netherite: Added in the 1.16 Nether Update, netherite tools are an upgrade to diamond and will not burn in lava.
Minecraft blocks and items.Cobblestone: The first block most players mine, cobblestone is the product of breaking stone, and it forms tools and furnaces.
Minecraft blocks and items.Crafting table: A crafting table opens a 3x3 grid for building. It's usually among the first things you make from wood.
Minecraft blocks and items.Furnace: Furnaces smelt ores and cook food with fuel. In the game, one coal item can smelt eight items.
Minecraft blocks and items.Elytra: Elytra are wings found in End cities that let you glide, and with fireworks you can boost your flight.
Minecraft blocks and items.Ender pearl: Throw an ender pearl to teleport where it lands, though it costs you some health from fall damage.
Minecraft blocks and items.Bedrock: Bedrock is the unbreakable bottom layer of the world in survival mode, found at the lowest depths.
Minecraft blocks and items.TNT: TNT explodes when lit, and chain reactions can carve huge craters. It's a favorite of players and map makers.
Minecraft blocks and items.Torch: Torches light areas and stop hostile mobs from spawning nearby. They're made from coal or charcoal and a stick.
Minecraft blocks and items.Pickaxe: The pickaxe is the key tool for mining stone and ores, and it can be crafted in wood, stone, iron, gold, diamond and netherite.
Minecraft blocks and items.Rupee: Rupees are the currency in The Legend of Zelda, so they belong to Nintendo's series, not Minecraft.
Minecraft blocks and items.Triforce: The Triforce is a golden triangle of power, wisdom and courage from The Legend of Zelda.
Minecraft blocks and items.Chaos Emerald: Chaos Emeralds are the gems Sonic collects to turn Super Sonic. They belong to the Sega series.
Minecraft blocks and items.Power Star: Power Stars are what Mario collects in Super Mario 64 and Galaxy, a Nintendo item.
Minecraft blocks and items.Poke Ball: The Poke Ball captures Pokemon. It's an item from Pokemon, not Minecraft.
Minecraft blocks and items.Master Sword: The Master Sword is Link's sacred blade in Zelda, said to repel evil. It's not found in Minecraft.
Minecraft blocks and items.Portal gun: The portal gun creates linked doorways in Valve's Portal games, with GLaDOS as its tester.
Minecraft blocks and items.Gravity gun: The gravity gun is a physics-grabbing tool from Half-Life 2, which can hurl objects at foes.
Minecraft blocks and items.Energy Tank: Energy Tanks are health upgrades in the Metroid series, and each adds 100 energy.
Minecraft blocks and items.Pac-Dot: Pac-Dots are the small pellets Pac-Man eats while evading ghosts, and they belong to Namco's game.
Minecraft blocks and items.Bob-omb: Bob-ombs are walking bombs in the Mario series, and they're not Minecraft items.

Things from medieval Europe.Knight: A mounted warrior, typically trained from boyhood as page and squire. A full suit of plate armour weighed about 20 to 25 kg, less than modern soldiers' kit.
Things from medieval Europe.Castle: Early castles were wooden "motte-and-bailey" forts that could be thrown up in days. Stone ones came later, and the spiral stairs usually turned clockwise.
Things from medieval Europe.Feudalism: A system in which lords gave land to vassals in return for military service. Its peasants were bound to the land they worked.
Things from medieval Europe.Serf: Unlike slaves, serfs could not be sold apart from the land, but they could not leave it either, and owed labour to the lord.
Things from medieval Europe.Jousting: A sport as much as warfare, with lances sometimes blunted for tournaments. The 1559 death of France's Henri II from a splinter helped end its popularity.
Things from medieval Europe.Crusades: A series of religious wars from 1095 onwards, aimed at taking Jerusalem and the Holy Land. The First Crusade captured it in 1099.
Things from medieval Europe.Black Death: The plague that reached Europe in 1347 and killed perhaps a third or more of the population. Its labour shortage ended up helping workers' wages.
Things from medieval Europe.Magna Carta: Sealed by King John in 1215 at Runnymede, it limited royal power. Its famous clause says no free man is punished without lawful judgment.
Things from medieval Europe.Monastery: Medieval monasteries preserved ancient writings by hand-copying them. Some monks also brewed beer and invented champagne-style techniques, such as at Hautvillers.
Things from medieval Europe.Trebuchet: A counterweight siege engine that could hurl stones of 100 kg or more. In one siege, rotting corpses were reportedly thrown to spread disease.
Things from medieval Europe.Chivalry: The knight's code of honour, courage and courtesy. It grew from military rules into ideals of romantic love and loyalty in medieval literature.
Things from medieval Europe.Guild: An association of craftsmen or merchants that set standards and prices, and trained apprentices. Over time they became powerful town institutions.
Things from medieval Europe.Squire: A young knight-in-training who carried arms and armour. After years of service he could be knighted, often for valour in battle.
Things from medieval Europe.Steam engine: Developed in the 1700s, with Watt's improvements arriving in the 1770s. It powered the Industrial Revolution, centuries after the Middle Ages.
Things from medieval Europe.Gladiator: Roman arena fighters, with the last Colosseum games around the 400s. They belong to antiquity, not medieval Europe.
Things from medieval Europe.Pharaoh: An ancient Egyptian king, whose rule ended with Cleopatra in 30 BC, over a thousand years before the medieval era.
Things from medieval Europe.Cowboy: A figure of the American West of the 1800s. The word and the job came centuries after the Middle Ages.
Things from medieval Europe.Telescope: Invented in the Netherlands in about 1608, then improved by Galileo. It came after the Middle Ages.
Things from medieval Europe.Railway: Steam railways appeared in the early 1800s. Medieval goods moved by cart, boat and pack animal.
Things from medieval Europe.Factory: Factories arose with the Industrial Revolution from the late 1700s. Medieval work was done in homes and workshops.
Things from medieval Europe.Electricity: The electric current was harnessed in the 1700s and 1800s. Medieval people knew static from amber, and lightning scared them.
Things from medieval Europe.Toga: The Roman citizen's garment, worn in antiquity. It was long out of fashion by the medieval period.
Things from medieval Europe.Dinosaur: Gone 66 million years before any human. The word "dinosaur" was coined only in 1842 by Richard Owen.
Things from medieval Europe.Pyramid: Built by Egyptians over 4,000 years ago. A medieval traveller could see them, but they were ancient wonders.

Polar explorers.Roald Amundsen: This Norwegian beat Scott to the South Pole in December 1911 by about five weeks, using sled dogs and skis.
Polar explorers.Robert Falcon Scott: He reached the South Pole in January 1912, only to find Amundsen's tent. He died with two companions on the way back.
Polar explorers.Ernest Shackleton: After his ship Endurance was crushed by ice in 1915, he got all 28 men home alive through an epic lifeboat voyage.
Polar explorers.Robert Peary: He claimed the North Pole in 1909, a claim historians have debated ever since.
Polar explorers.Fridtjof Nansen: He let his ship Fram freeze into drifting Arctic ice in 1893. He later won the Nobel Peace Prize for refugee work.
Polar explorers.Douglas Mawson: This Australian geologist survived a deadly 1912 trek across Antarctica alone after both companions died.
Polar explorers.Richard Byrd: An American admiral who led airplane-supported Antarctic expeditions from 1928. His 1926 North Pole flight claim is doubted.
Polar explorers.Matthew Henson: Peary's partner on seven expeditions. He spoke the Inuit language and was the better dog driver and craftsman.
Polar explorers.John Franklin: He vanished in 1845 searching for the Northwest Passage. The wrecks of Erebus and Terror were found in 2014 and 2016.
Polar explorers.Ranulph Fiennes: This British adventurer led the Transglobe Expedition, the first to reach both poles by surface travel.
Polar explorers.Christopher Columbus: His voyages crossed the warm Atlantic to the Caribbean. He was no polar explorer.
Polar explorers.Magellan: His fleet made the first circumnavigation, though he died in the Philippines in 1521. His route stayed in warm waters.
Polar explorers.Vasco da Gama: He found the sea route from Europe to India in 1498, round Africa, not the poles.
Polar explorers.Marco Polo: The Venetian merchant traveled overland to China in the 1200s. He never went to polar regions.
Polar explorers.David Livingstone: A Scottish missionary who explored central Africa, and the first European to see Victoria Falls.
Polar explorers.Hernan Cortes: He conquered the Aztec Empire in 1519 to 1521, a hot-country campaign and nothing polar.
Polar explorers.Francisco Pizarro: Conqueror of the Inca Empire, in the Andes. Mountains, yes; poles, no.
Polar explorers.Balboa: He was the first European to see the Pacific from the Americas, in 1513, after crossing Panama's jungles.
Polar explorers.Ibn Battuta: The Moroccan scholar covered roughly 120,000 km across the Islamic world in the 1300s, but no polar lands.
Polar explorers.John Cabot: He reached North America's coast around 1497. Newfoundland is cold, but he did not go polar.
Polar explorers.Zheng He: This Chinese admiral led giant treasure fleets to Africa in the early 1400s, nowhere near the poles.
Polar explorers.Samuel de Champlain: He founded Quebec in 1608. Canada is cold, but he was no polar explorer.
Polar explorers.Hernando de Soto: He explored the American Southeast and crossed the Mississippi in 1541, in warm country.
Polar explorers.Meriwether Lewis: With William Clark he crossed America from 1804 to 1806 and reached the Pacific. No poles were involved.

Things that have keys.Piano: Modern ones have 88 keys, 52 white and 36 black, and the piano's name comes from 'pianoforte', soft-loud, referring to its dynamic range.
Things that have keys.Typewriter: The QWERTY layout was designed to keep commonly used letter bars from jamming, and Christopher Sholes patented the first practical typewriter in 1868.
Things that have keys.Laptop: Its keyboard keys have a tiny scissor mechanism under each one, and the first portable computers appeared in the early 1980s.
Things that have keys.Accordion: It has piano-style keys on one side and buttons for chords on the other, and air from the bellows passes over metal reeds.
Things that have keys.Pipe organ: Its keys, in several rows called manuals, open valves that let air into pipes, and the biggest ones have tens of thousands of pipes.
Things that have keys.Calculator: Pocket versions appeared in the early 1970s, and the first ones were expensive, costing the equivalent of hundreds of dollars.
Things that have keys.Saxophone: Despite being brass, a sax is a woodwind because it has a single reed, and keys cover its holes. Adolphe Sax invented it around 1840.
Things that have keys.Flute: Keys cover holes along the tube, and the Boehm system of the 1830s gave the modern flute its clear and in-tune sound.
Things that have keys.Clarinet: Its keys and rings cover holes, and the instrument has a distinctive single reed. It also can play across a very wide range.
Things that have keys.Computer keyboard: Keys press switches to send signals, and the layout inherits the typewriter's QWERTY, a century and a half later.
Things that have keys.Guitar: Trap: it has frets and strings, and tuning pegs, but no keys, though the 'key' in music is another meaning.
Things that have keys.Violin: Trap: it is played with a bow on strings and has no keys, though some call its tuning pegs keys.
Things that have keys.Drum: Trap: a stretched skin struck with sticks or hands, so no keys, but tuned percussion like xylophones have bars.
Things that have keys.Trumpet: Trap: it has three valves operated by pistons, not keys.
Things that have keys.Harp: Trap: it has strings plucked by hand and pedals, but no keys.
Things that have keys.Ukulele: Trap: a four-stringed instrument that has frets, not keys.
Things that have keys.Tambourine: Trap: a frame drum with jingles, and no keys.
Things that have keys.Banjo: Trap: a banjo has strings and a drum-like body, and no keys.
Things that have keys.Cello: Trap: bowed strings with no keys, though bigger than a violin.
Things that have keys.Triangle: Trap: a bent metal bar struck with a beater, and it needs no keys.
Things that have keys.Trombone: Trap: it has a slide that changes pitch, so no keys or valves.
Things that have keys.Computer mouse: Trap: it has buttons and a wheel, but a mouse is not a keyboard, so it has no keys.
Things that have keys.Harmonica: Trap: you breathe through holes in the instrument, and it has no keys, though harmonicas are sold in different keys.
Things that have keys.Tuba: Trap: a large brass instrument played with valves, not keys.

Things you shouldn't put in a microwave.Fork: Sparks fly because the electric field concentrates at the sharp tines, causing arcing that can damage the oven.
Things you shouldn't put in a microwave.Aluminum foil: Small smooth pieces are sometimes tolerated, but crumpled foil with sharp edges can spark and even catch fire.
Things you shouldn't put in a microwave.Steel travel mug: The metal walls reflect microwaves, so the drink inside barely warms and the oven may be damaged.
Things you shouldn't put in a microwave.Egg in its shell: Steam builds up inside and can burst the egg, sometimes even after it has left the oven.
Things you shouldn't put in a microwave.Cast iron pan: Metal reflects the waves instead of heating, so food stays cool while the pan risks sparks.
Things you shouldn't put in a microwave.Smartphone: Don't run a microwave with a phone inside; the oven's metal mesh acts as a Faraday cage that blocks signal.
Things you shouldn't put in a microwave.Teaspoon: Small metal items can spark depending on their shape, so even a harmless-looking spoon is best kept out.
Things you shouldn't put in a microwave.Metal bowl: Metal reflects microwaves and can cause arcing, which is why you need microwave-safe dishes.
Things you shouldn't put in a microwave.Gold-rimmed plate: Even a thin gold or silver rim can arc and scorch, leaving a permanent burn mark on the plate.
Things you shouldn't put in a microwave.Tin can: Sealed cans can burst, and the metal walls reflect the waves instead of heating the food.
Things you shouldn't put in a microwave.Metal twist tie: The thin wire inside a bread-bag tie can spark and ignite the paper around it.
Things you shouldn't put in a microwave.Popcorn bag: Percy Spencer reportedly tested popcorn first when he discovered microwave cooking, and the idea stuck.
Things you shouldn't put in a microwave.Leftover pizza: Microwaves make crust chewy because the water inside it heats first, which is why reheated pizza gets soggy.
Things you shouldn't put in a microwave.Glass bowl: Heat-safe glass bowls are fine because glass lets microwaves pass through to the food inside.
Things you shouldn't put in a microwave.Plain ceramic mug: Plain ceramic is fine so long as it has no metallic paint or trim.
Things you shouldn't put in a microwave.Frozen peas: Frozen peas heat quickly in a microwave, since small pieces warm fast.
Things you shouldn't put in a microwave.Baked potato: Pierce the skin of a baked potato first, so steam can escape instead of building up and bursting it.
Things you shouldn't put in a microwave.TV dinner: Swanson introduced the 'TV dinner' in 1953 after a huge surplus of Thanksgiving turkey needed using.
Things you shouldn't put in a microwave.Oatmeal: Stir oatmeal partway so it heats evenly, since microwaves leave hot and cold spots.
Things you shouldn't put in a microwave.Soup: Stir soup halfway, since liquids can superheat and boil over when disturbed.
Things you shouldn't put in a microwave.Butter: Butter melts quickly, so cover it to avoid spatter.
Things you shouldn't put in a microwave.Paper towel: Plain white paper towels are fine in a microwave and absorb splatter.
Things you shouldn't put in a microwave.Corn on the cob: Corn husks steam naturally in the microwave, locking in moisture.
Things you shouldn't put in a microwave.Leftover rice: Reheated rice is safe only if it was cooled quickly, since spores of Bacillus cereus survive cooking.

Furniture designed for sitting.Chair: Chairs were once a mark of rank; the word chairman comes from the person who sat in the one chair while others used benches.
Furniture designed for sitting.Stool: With no back or arms, a stool is the simplest seat, and three legs keep it steady on uneven ground without wobbling.
Furniture designed for sitting.Sofa: The word came from Arabic suffa, a raised platform for sitting, and reached English by way of Turkish in the 1600s.
Furniture designed for sitting.Bench: Park benches are a rare place where strangers share a seat, and the word bench also gave us the judge's bench in court.
Furniture designed for sitting.Bean bag: The famous bean bag chair, the Sacco, was designed in Italy in 1968, and it was originally stuffed with polystyrene beads.
Furniture designed for sitting.Rocking chair: Benjamin Franklin is often credited with the rocking chair in America, though that story is uncertain and the design is older.
Furniture designed for sitting.Recliner: The recliner traces back to a 1920s chair that two cousins built in Michigan for their porch before it became the La-Z-Boy.
Furniture designed for sitting.Armchair: An armchair critic is someone who offers views from comfort without direct experience, a phrase from the late 1800s.
Furniture designed for sitting.Loveseat: Early loveseats were wide enough to fit a woman in a full skirt, and only later became known as seats for two.
Furniture designed for sitting.Bar stool: Bar stools are tall because bars are high, and the footrest ring around the legs is there to give your heels a place to rest.
Furniture designed for sitting.Pew: Pews became common in churches only in the later Middle Ages, and before that, many worshippers simply stood or sat on the floor.
Furniture designed for sitting.Futon: The Japanese futon is a thin padded mattress laid out on the floor and folded away, quite unlike the Western sofa bed.
Furniture designed for sitting.Wardrobe: A wardrobe stores clothes, not people. The word comes from old French for guarding robes, and you stand and hang things in it.
Furniture designed for sitting.Bookcase: It holds books, not people. A fully stocked one can weigh enough that it should be anchored to the wall.
Furniture designed for sitting.Dresser: A dresser stores clothes in drawers. Sitting on one is a common habit, but it is not what it was built for.
Furniture designed for sitting.Nightstand: A small table beside the bed for a lamp and a book. Medieval versions were cabinets that held a chamber pot.
Furniture designed for sitting.Coffee table: A low table for cups and magazines. The modern coffee table came from Japanese low tables in the late 1800s.
Furniture designed for sitting.Desk: It is a work surface, and you sit at a desk, not on it. The word comes from Latin for a table for writing.
Furniture designed for sitting.Cupboard: A cupboard holds items. The name originally meant a board, or table, for cups and plates.
Furniture designed for sitting.Sideboard: A sideboard is a long low cabinet for serving dishes and storage, not for sitting on.
Furniture designed for sitting.Coat rack: It holds coats on pegs or hooks, not you. Pegs on a rack have existed since long before modern homes.
Furniture designed for sitting.Filing cabinet: Built to hold papers in drawers, not people. The vertical filing cabinet became an office staple around the 1890s.
Furniture designed for sitting.Chest of drawers: A chest of drawers holds clothes. It evolved from the medieval trunk, with drawers added in the 1600s.
Furniture designed for sitting.Display cabinet: It shows off china and collectables behind glass. You admire it rather than sit on it.

Types of brush.Toothbrush: The first bristle toothbrush appeared in China around 1498, using stiff hairs from a hog's neck on a bamboo handle.
Types of brush.Hairbrush: Brushing 100 strokes a night is a myth; too much brushing can actually damage hair and cause breakage.
Types of brush.Paintbrush: Artist's finest brushes, called kolinsky sable, use hair from a Siberian weasel, not from the sable at all.
Types of brush.Toilet brush: Toilet brushes usually sit in a holder, and their bristles are stiff and angled to scrub under the rim.
Types of brush.Scrub brush: Scrub brushes have short, stiff bristles and a handle shaped to be gripped hard, built to take on grout and burnt-on grime.
Types of brush.Pastry brush: A pastry brush paints on egg wash, which gives baked goods that glossy golden shine.
Types of brush.Shaving brush: Shaving brushes made of badger hair hold a lot of water, making a thick lather that lifts the whiskers.
Types of brush.Makeup brush: Makeup brushes are best washed weekly, because bacteria and oils build up in the bristles.
Types of brush.Bottle brush: The bottle brush has a cousin in nature: the bottlebrush plant of Australia, whose flowers look exactly like one.
Types of brush.Nail brush: Nail brushes scrub under fingernails, and surgeons used them to scrub before surgery before gloves were common.
Types of brush.Wire brush: Wire brushes strip rust and old paint, and steel bristles can even clean a hot barbecue grate.
Types of brush.Comb: A comb is a bristleless toothed tool; combs have been found dating back some 5,000 years.
Types of brush.Sponge: Natural sponges are animals, and the porous skeleton of the sea sponge was used to wash for thousands of years.
Types of brush.Mop: A mop uses loose strands or a flat pad to wipe a floor and has no bristles, so it is not a brush.
Types of brush.Rake: A rake has stiff tines that gather leaves; there are no fine bristles, so it is not a brush.
Types of brush.Feather duster: Feather dusters trap dust with static electricity, though ostrich feathers are a luxury version.
Types of brush.Squeegee: A squeegee uses a flat rubber blade, which pushes water off glass rather than sweeping with bristles.
Types of brush.Rag: A rag is just a scrap of cloth, and old-time papermakers used rags as the main source of paper pulp.
Types of brush.Loofah: A loofah is the dried fibrous inside of a gourd plant, not a sea sponge.
Types of brush.Cotton swab: Cotton swabs are used for ears but doctors warn against pushing them in, as that can pack wax deeper.
Types of brush.Spatula: A spatula is a flat blade for lifting, flipping or scraping and has no bristles.
Types of brush.Paint roller: A paint roller was invented in 1940 by Canadian Norman Breakey and lays paint on with a fuzzy cylinder.
Types of brush.Pumice stone: Pumice is volcanic rock so full of gas bubbles that it floats on water.
Types of brush.Steel wool: Steel wool is a bundle of very fine steel threads; it is an abrasive pad, not a brush.

Things that have a motor.Blender: A blender motor spins its blades at many thousands of revolutions per minute, enough to pulverize ice.
Things that have a motor.Vacuum cleaner: Hubert Cecil Booth built the first powered vacuum cleaner in 1901, a horse-drawn machine that was parked outside buildings.
Things that have a motor.Car: Electric cars date to the 1800s, and around 1900 they competed with gasoline cars in popularity.
Things that have a motor.Ceiling fan: Philip Diehl introduced the electric ceiling fan in 1882, adding a motor to the idea of hanging blades.
Things that have a motor.Washing machine: The motor spins the drum, and many modern machines get their power from a drive that is surprisingly efficient.
Things that have a motor.Electric drill: The first portable electric drill was made in Germany by Wilhelm Fein in 1895, and it was a heavy beast.
Things that have a motor.Hair dryer: French stylist Alexandre Godefroy built an early electric hair dryer in 1890, used mostly in salons at first.
Things that have a motor.Food processor: The Cuisinart, introduced in America in the early 1970s by Carl Sontheimer, popularized the food processor.
Things that have a motor.Electric toothbrush: A Swiss dentist invented the Broxodent in 1954, partly for patients who had trouble brushing manually.
Things that have a motor.Garage door opener: Remote garage door openers date to 1926, and the modern radio control version followed decades later.
Things that have a motor.Escalator: Jesse Reno's moving staircase debuted at Coney Island in 1896, carrying riders up a sloping belt.
Things that have a motor.Tumble dryer: Early dryers were hand-cranked perforated drums turned over a fire, and the electric motor spared people the effort.
Things that have a motor.Toaster: The pop-up toaster was patented in 1919 by Charles Strite, but it is run by a spring and timer, not by a motor.
Things that have a motor.Kettle: An electric kettle boils water with a heating element, which has no moving parts and so needs no motor.
Things that have a motor.Clothes iron: A modern iron has a heating plate and thermostat, but no motor, though early irons were just heated metal.
Things that have a motor.Bicycle: A bicycle is powered by your legs, and only becomes motorized if it is converted into an e-bike or moped.
Things that have a motor.Skateboard: Skateboards began in California in the 1950s, when surfers put wheels on boards to ride when waves were flat.
Things that have a motor.Rowing boat: A rowing boat is powered by oars and muscle, and has been for thousands of years.
Things that have a motor.Candle: A candle burns wax with a wick and has nothing mechanical in it at all.
Things that have a motor.Hair straightener: A flat iron heats ceramic plates and is all heat and no motion.
Things that have a motor.Electric blanket: An electric blanket has thin heating wires woven in, and they warm by resistance rather than a motor.
Things that have a motor.Light bulb: Thomas Edison's bulb of 1879 made light with a glowing filament, no moving parts needed.
Things that have a motor.Waffle maker: A waffle maker heats two grooved plates and needs no motor, just a hinge.
Things that have a motor.Sailboat: A sailboat gets its power from the wind, though many carry a small auxiliary motor for harbors.

Things on a credit card.Card number: The first digit shows the network, 4 for Visa and 5 for Mastercard, and the last digit is a check number computed with the Luhn algorithm.
Things on a credit card.Expiry date: Cards expire so the issuer can swap out old chips and numbers, a security refresh every few years.
Things on a credit card.Cardholder name: Embossed names were once pressed onto carbon paper by imprinter machines, which is why older cards have raised lettering.
Things on a credit card.Chip: EMV chips create a unique code for every payment, which makes copied card data far less useful than the old stripe.
Things on a credit card.Bank logo: The issuing bank's logo shows who actually lends the money, which can differ from the network on the card.
Things on a credit card.Security code: The three or four digits are not stored in the magnetic stripe, which stops a thief with only the card details.
Things on a credit card.Magnetic stripe: The black stripe stores data as tiny magnetized regions, and swiping it was the main method until chips took over.
Things on a credit card.Signature strip: The panel is on the back so that shops can compare your signature, though few actually check it any more.
Things on a credit card.Network logo: Visa, Mastercard and others run the payment network, and the interlocking circles of Mastercard are among the most recognized logos.
Things on a credit card.Contactless symbol: The four curved lines mean you can tap to pay by radio, and the chip only works within a few centimeters.
Things on a credit card.PIN: A trap: the PIN is never printed on the card, but is sent separately to the owner, and the chip checks it.
Things on a credit card.Account balance: A credit card does not hold a balance, which stays on the bank's computers.
Things on a credit card.Home address: Your address is tied to the account, not printed on the plastic, which can be lost.
Things on a credit card.Date of birth: A card has no date of birth on it, so shops can only confirm age from other ID.
Things on a credit card.Credit limit: The limit is kept by the issuer, and the card itself never shows what it is.
Things on a credit card.Email address: Email is held by the bank for statements, never printed on the card.
Things on a credit card.Password: Passwords would be a security risk if printed, so they stay in your head or password manager.
Things on a credit card.Credit score: A credit score is calculated by a bureau and is not found on any card.
Things on a credit card.Spending history: The card keeps no purchase history, while your bank's statements do.
Things on a credit card.Salary: Your salary is none of the card's business, and the issuer only sees your income at application.
Things on a credit card.Bank statement: The statement is a monthly document from the bank, now mostly sent online.
Things on a credit card.Mother's maiden name: This is a classic security question, and it is a poor one since it is often public record.
Things on a credit card.Interest rate: The rate is in the cardholder agreement, and it is never printed on the card.
Things on a credit card.Shoe size: No card needs your shoe size, though a retailer's loyalty card might one day.

Things for a barbecue.Tongs: Long tongs keep your hand away from the fire, and many grill masters prefer them to forks since they don't pierce meat and release juices.
Things for a barbecue.Grill brush: Cleaning a grill with a wire brush is common, but loose bristles can break off and end up in food, so many cooks now prefer alternatives.
Things for a barbecue.Charcoal: Charcoal is wood heated without air. Its use as fuel goes back thousands of years, and it burns hotter and cleaner than raw wood.
Things for a barbecue.Lighter fluid: Lighter fluid is flammable, so it must burn off before cooking or the meat can pick up a chemical taste.
Things for a barbecue.Skewers: Skewers are among the oldest ways to grill. Soaking wooden ones in water prevents them from burning.
Things for a barbecue.Basting brush: A basting brush spreads sauce while grilling. Silicone ones don't shed bristles and wash easily.
Things for a barbecue.Meat thermometer: A meat thermometer is the only reliable way to check doneness. Chicken is safe at 165 F (74 C).
Things for a barbecue.Grill fork: A grill fork flips and holds meat. Piercing steak with it lets precious juices escape.
Things for a barbecue.Propane tank: Propane tanks hold fuel as liquid under pressure, and a standard barbecue tank holds about 20 pounds.
Things for a barbecue.Chimney starter: A chimney starter is a metal cylinder that lights charcoal with crumpled paper, with no lighter fluid needed.
Things for a barbecue.Grill spatula: Long-handled spatulas flip burgers from a safe distance, as the heat at a grill can be intense.
Things for a barbecue.Whisk: A whisk blends batters and eggs in the kitchen. Nothing needs whisking on a barbecue.
Things for a barbecue.Rolling pin: A rolling pin is for pastry and dough. A grill's menu rarely includes rolled dough.
Things for a barbecue.Cookie cutter: Cookie cutters shape dough. You'd need an oven for what they produce, not a grill.
Things for a barbecue.Muffin tin: A muffin tin shapes batter into cupcakes. It can go on a grill in a pinch, but it's an oven tool.
Things for a barbecue.Toaster: A toaster is for bread slices on a kitchen counter, where electricity is on tap. A grill burns real fuel.
Things for a barbecue.Microwave: A microwave heats by exciting water molecules, which is the opposite of grilling and its charred flavor.
Things for a barbecue.Blender: A blender mixes smoothies and sauces and needs a power point, so it's not a barbecue tool.
Things for a barbecue.Ice cream scoop: An ice cream scoop portions dessert. It's a kitchen tool even in a summer barbecue.
Things for a barbecue.Cake stand: A cake stand shows off a dessert. It's pretty but not part of a grill.
Things for a barbecue.Teapot: A teapot belongs on a stove or table. Nobody brews tea on a barbecue.
Things for a barbecue.Salad spinner: A salad spinner dries lettuce with centrifugal force. It's a trap, since salad is common at barbecues but the spinner stays in the kitchen.
Things for a barbecue.Piping bag: A piping bag decorates cakes and pastries and it's a baking item, not a barbecue one.
Things for a barbecue.Rice cooker: A rice cooker steams rice with an automatic switch-off. It's a kitchen appliance, not something near a grill.

Things banned from carry-on luggage.Chainsaw: Security won't let a chainsaw through the cabin, though some airlines allow one in checked bags if it's drained of fuel and oil.
Things banned from carry-on luggage.Fireworks: Fireworks are explosives, and flight rules forbid them in both carry-on and checked bags, since a spark in a cargo hold is a disaster.
Things banned from carry-on luggage.Machete: A machete is a blade far over the length limits, so it must go in checked luggage, sheathed, or stay home.
Things banned from carry-on luggage.Gasoline: Gasoline is a flammable liquid that is banned from carry-on and checked bags, because its vapors can ignite at very low temperatures.
Things banned from carry-on luggage.Flare gun: A flare gun can only travel in checked baggage, unloaded and in a locked case, with the flares themselves barred from the plane.
Things banned from carry-on luggage.Hatchet: A hatchet's blade is too big for the cabin, but it can go in checked luggage if you cover the edge well.
Things banned from carry-on luggage.Baseball bat: A baseball bat is a banned blunt instrument in carry-on, even though stadiums let fans carry souvenir bats home.
Things banned from carry-on luggage.Crowbar: The crowbar counts as a tool that could double as a weapon, so it belongs in checked baggage, not at your seat.
Things banned from carry-on luggage.Sword: Even antique or ceremonial swords are banned in the cabin, and many countries have strict rules for checking them too.
Things banned from carry-on luggage.Spear: A spear's long shaft and point make it a firm no in the cabin, and it often has to fit special oversized baggage rules.
Things banned from carry-on luggage.Bear spray: Bear spray is pressurized pepper spray, so airports ban it, though a small amount of self-defense spray can go in checked bags.
Things banned from carry-on luggage.Gallon of milk: A trap: milk is a liquid, and in most countries containers over 100 ml can't pass security, so a full gallon is stopped.
Things banned from carry-on luggage.Passport: Your passport is the one thing you must keep with you, as airlines won't let you board international flights without it.
Things banned from carry-on luggage.Paperback: Paperbacks are fine in carry-on, and a few airports even have book swap shelves for travelers to leave and grab reads.
Things banned from carry-on luggage.Phone: Phones are welcome in the cabin, and in fact the lithium batteries inside are safer with you than stowed in the cargo hold.
Things banned from carry-on luggage.Laptop: Laptops are allowed, but at many airports you must pull them out of the bag so the scanner can see them clearly.
Things banned from carry-on luggage.Headphones: Headphones are allowed, but noise-canceling ones work by creating sound waves that cancel engine drone, which is why they help on flights.
